Estonia Faces Sharp Economic Downturn as Currency Slides

TALLINN, June 19 — Estonia is grappling with a severe economic crisis as the kroon tumbled to historic lows against the euro and U.S. dollar, sparking concerns of widespread instability and disrupting daily commerce across the Baltic nation.

The kroon, which had traded steadily for years, lost more than 20 percent of its value in the past month, according to data from the Central Bank of Estonia. The sudden slide has led to a spike in import prices, with inflation rising to an estimated annual rate of 18 percent in May, according to preliminary figures from the National Statistics Board.

“The drop in the kroon’s value is unprecedented in our recent history,” said Finance Minister Marko Laar. “We are working closely with our partners in the European Union and the International Monetary Fund to stabilize the situation.”

The currency collapse has prompted many retailers to raise prices sharply, particularly for imported goods such as food, fuel, and electronics. “We’ve had to adjust our prices almost daily,” said Maarika Kallas, manager of the Sild Market grocery chain in Tartu. “Customers are frustrated and worried about what tomorrow will bring.”

Labor groups say companies have begun laying off workers as businesses struggle to manage costs and declining consumer demand. The Estonian Trade Union Confederation reported that at least 4,000 jobs have been cut since the start of June, with more at risk if the crisis persists.

Local analysts warn that the crisis could deepen unless swift action is taken. “Confidence in the kroon has eroded, and if capital continues to flow out, we may see further depreciation,” said Jaanus Peets, chief economist at Läänemere Bank.

The government has called an emergency session of parliament to discuss potential interventions, including currency controls and financial aid for vulnerable households.
